Well for one many countries have institutions that seek to stop monopolies from forming in private sector. Let's say two market leaders want to merge which would mean one company would now control the entire (or absolute majority) of the market. Governmental intervention can stop this from happening. Then governments often try to break up oligopolies (commonly called cartels) where the market leaders enact a secret agreement and carve up their spheres of influence and secretly agree on prices and products. Unfortunately success here has been limited since it's always hard to prove anything. The EU has previously given out big fines to some pharma and tech companies. Unfortunately the fines while seeming big in absolute terms were very small compared to the profits of the companies.

When laissez-faire advocates boast about how the unfettered free market always leads to the most competitive and efficient system they completely forget (or deliberately don't mention) the tendency for cartels and monopolies to appear. Governmental intervention is a prerequisite for a free market, it may sound like an oxymoron but it's the truth.

Then I guess it's a question of what the word competetive means in this context. Having the products of a domestic company succeed on the world market? Give them subsidies or tax breaks. Having a failing industry remain competetive on the domestic market? Raise tariffs for foreign goods. It really depends on the context.
